The single-pipe form may have developed from polyphonic instruments that dropped their drone pipe. Its use began in France and spread to Germany after the seventeenth century, and it was established on the European musical scene by around 1700. The Nuremberg maker Johann Christoph Denner added two keys; because the placing of the fingerholes limited overblowing, the range was only a twelfth, and instruments were therefore made in different sizes. Over the next twenty years or so, a moved back key, a small added pipe to help overblowing, a lengthened body, a changed bell and a lower key to add high notes turned it into the Baroque clarinet. Around 1800 the chalumeau dropped out of the repertoire.

The chalumeau is a single-reed woodwind of the late Baroque and early Classical periods, an aerophone with the Hornbostel–Sachs number 422.211. It has a cylindrical body and eight fingerholes (seven in front and one at the back for the thumb), and a wide mouthpiece carrying a cane reed separate from the body; when played it overblows a twelfth. The instrument comes from France and later spread to Germany, was established on the European music scene by about 1700, and was used in opera and oratorio at the Habsburg court; it was also a folk instrument, and it is the forerunner of the modern clarinet.
夏呂莫單簧管的簧片為蘆竹製，屬分離式單簧。現存原件多數琴身以黃楊木製成，並有兩個: The chalumeau's reed is of cane and is a separate single reed. Most surviving originals have a body of boxwood and two opposed keys worked by the left thumb and index finger. The mouthpiece is large, the reed usually sits on top, and as it vibrates it presses close to the upper lip. Apart from the reed, the body wood and the key arrangement, the source does not state the materials of the mouthpiece, the keys or the other parts.
夏呂莫單簧管見於巴洛克晚期與古典早期歐洲音樂，源自法國後傳入德國。哈布斯堡宮廷歌: The chalumeau appears in European music of the late Baroque and early Classical periods, coming from France and later spreading to Germany. It was used in opera and oratorio at the Habsburg court, and composers such as Fux, Vivaldi and Telemann wrote for it. Graupner wrote overture suites, concertos, church cantatas and trio sonatas for its different sizes, often for two or three played together. In 1706 Amsterdam published duets for two chalumeaux, and ballet also used the instrument in the 1770s.

The body has eight fingerholes, seven in front and one at the back for the thumb; surviving instruments have two further opposed keys, worked by the left thumb and index finger. The airstream sets the single reed vibrating, and the cylindrical bore makes the pitch low and allows overblowing a twelfth. A beginner should first learn the holes and keys, then practise a steady airstream and overblowing; because of the keys the range is narrow, and it has to be adjusted to instruments of different sizes.
